cau_loi: September 1666. From an alehouse on this bank, a man watches the City burn.
“A most horrid malicious bloody flame,” he writes, “not like the fine flame of an ordinary fire.”

cau_loi: This is the City of London, seen from Bankside, across the Thames.
Among the towers stands one dome — and much of this skyline is shaped to keep it in view.
We are standing near where Samuel Pepys stood on the second night of the Great Fire.

cau_loi: London has burned to the ground twice.
Twice, it got the chance to start over.
And twice, it rebuilt itself on its old, crooked streets.

cau_loi: The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bludworth, is overwhelmed.
Pepys finds him in Cannon Street, a handkerchief round his neck: "Lord, what can I do?
I am spent.
People will not obey me."
That afternoon, the King and his brother James, Duke of York, take to the river in the royal barge, ordering houses pulled down “apace”.

cau_loi: London Bridge survives.

At two in the afternoon, it takes the Royal Exchange — the City's trading floor.

cau_loi: John Evelyn walks the burning streets that night.
The sky, he writes, is "like the top of a burning oven"; the noise is "like a hideous storm" — the cracking of the flames, the fall of towers, houses and churches.

cau_loi: Tuesday, the fourth.
The fire climbs Ludgate Hill to St Paul's Cathedral, wrapped in wooden scaffolding for repairs.
Six days before the fire, John Evelyn and Christopher Wren had surveyed its decay — and proposed crowning it with a dome.
By evening, the great church is ablaze.

cau_loi: In the west, the fire crosses the Fleet and runs down Fleet Street, as far as the Temple.
Only now are houses blown up with gunpowder to open firebreaks — first in Tower Street, near the Tower.
At the Navy Office, Pepys and a colleague dig a pit in the garden for their wine — and Pepys buries his Parmesan cheese.
In the last days of the fire, the King and the Duke work the fire-lines themselves — “even laboring in person,” Evelyn writes.

cau_loi: Within days, Christopher Wren hands the King a new City on paper — straight avenues, open squares, a grid.
John Evelyn draws another.
Robert Hooke, a third.
None of them is built.

cau_loi: Every plot in the burnt City has its owners — and the people who have lost their homes cannot afford to wait years for it all to be redrawn.
So Parliament moves faster.
From late February 1667, a special Fire Court sits at Clifford's Inn, settling disputes between landlords and tenants.
In its first year, it decides three hundred and seventy-four cases.

The St Paul's Heights still apply, alongside a set of protected views across London — the farthest from a hill in Richmond Park, ten miles away.
The Leadenhall Building tapers as it rises, so that from Fleet Street, the dome still has open sky behind it.

cau_loi: From Bankside tonight, you can stand roughly where Pepys stood, and look across at the same streets.
London burned twice.
Twice, it could have started over.
Twice, it kept its old streets.
And the skyline it built still bends around the one building it chose, again and again, to keep in view.
